1:
Five of the voices open on the same complaint, and it is about a word. Ellicott holds that the noun here is peculiar to the New Testament and a few passages of the Greek Old Testament, not to be found in any heathen writer, and that "charity," which now signifies tolerance or almsgiving, is an insufficient rendering that destroys the force of the third verse; the Latin took it because the ordinary word for love was too suggestive of fleshly affection, and perhaps it was hoped the English would grow into the larger sense; the experiment has not succeeded, and the word has never become acclimatised to this chapter. Clarke presses the same point to a contradiction: on the received rendering the apostle says that though a man have the utmost charity and act throughout by its dictates, if he have not charity it profits him nothing. He traces the descent, Wiclif taking it from the Vulgate and later revisers restoring it after Coverdale, Cranmer and the Geneva had put love. Calvin reproduces that history and blames the last revisers for abandoning a sound correction. Robertson says only that the Latin word is wholly inadequate, and Henry that most men understand by it almsgiving, which is not what is meant.

Calvin will not accept even the chapter division, calling it so absurd that he could not refrain from changing it, since the detached sentence closing the previous chapter belongs with what follows and is completed by it; he supposes a transcriber's mistake. The others let it stand and agree on the shape within it, Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott dividing the chapter the same way: the greatest gifts worthless without love, then love described, then gifts shown transient against what endures. What strikes Ellicott is where the passage sits. He finds it remarkable as coming from Paul rather than from John, and remarkable for standing in an atmosphere of controversy between stretches of close argument, which suggests to him a sudden inspiration breaking in; he calls the chapter the baptismal service of love, the place where love receives its Christian name. Robertson puts it as a figure, that it comes like a sweet bell between the jangling noise of the gifts on either side, and adds that it is a pity to pull the rose to pieces petal by petal. Tongues are named first, Ellicott and Henry agree, precisely because the Corinthians valued that gift most.

The tongues of angels are not a figure invented here. Lightfoot cites the rabbinic boast that Rabban Jochanan ben Zaccai had left out no branch of learning, the speech of devils, of palms and of angels included; Clarke reports the same tradition, adding that the tongues of men meant among them the seventy languages of the nations. On the instrument, Lightfoot describes two balls of brass struck one against another with neither measure nor tone, and notes the same verb used of the weeping and wailing at a deathbed. Wesley says it was two pieces of hollow brass giving a tinkling with little variety of sound, and Ellicott that the brass is not a trumpet but a plate of metal that can only make noise. The last clause of the third verse divides them. Clarke lays out the manuscript evidence for reading "that I may boast" instead of "to be burned," with Jerome and the Alexandrian codex behind it; Robertson accepts the boasting reading outright, while Ellicott calls it strange and thinks it weakens the passage, since what empties the sacrifice is not a wrong cause but the absence of love. Barnes observes that no Christian is known to have been burned as a martyr so early, and Calvin that the tyrants then used the sword, Nero excepted. Gill matches the giving of goods with rabbis who distributed all they had, and asks what it availed them.
4:
Ellicott says the apostle now attempts what he means us to feel is impossible, an adequate description of love, and does it by alternating positive traits with denials of evil ones. Chrysostom sees a painter at work, adorning the image with the parts of virtue as with colours and fitting the members together exactly, and warns the reader not to pass the words over quickly but to weigh each, so as to know both the treasure and the art. Calvin denies that the praise is praise only: it is meant to show what love's offices are, chiefly how it preserves the unity of the church, and he has no doubt the list was also an indirect reproof, a contrast in which the Corinthians might recognise their own faults by their contraries. Barnes reads it the same way, observing that every illustration is drawn from conduct toward others rather than toward God, because what needed correcting there was contention, suspicion, unkind judging, envy and boasting. Robertson calls the four verses a marvellous rhapsody. Chrysostom asks why long-suffering should stand first and answers that it is the root of all self-denial.

On that first word Chrysostom is at his most vehement. Long-suffering is more secure than a strong city, an invincible weapon and an impregnable tower; a spark falling into the deep does the water no injury and is itself quenched, and so whatever falls on such a soul quickly vanishes without disturbing it. Name armies, money, horses, walls, arms, and you have named nothing like it: a man encompassed with those is upset by anger like a worthless child, while this man lies in a harbour of profound calm. Surround him with loss and you have not moved the rock, insult him and you have not shaken the tower, bruise him with stripes and you have not wounded the adamant. Clarke renders the word as having a long mind, to the end of which neither trials nor provocations can reach, and Wesley in almost the same terms, that it bears the weakness and errors of the children of God and the malice of the children of the world, and not for a time but to the end. Barnes glosses it as slowness to anger, opposed to irritability; Henry says it will rather wait and wish for a brother's reformation than fly out at his conduct.

Kindness gives Robertson a rarity: the verb turns up nowhere but in Clement of Rome and Eusebius, and may be Paul's coinage or a vernacular word lying ready for him. Henry has the law of kindness in her lips, her heart large and her hand open, not merely seizing opportunities of doing good but searching for them; Barnes notes Tindale's rendering, courteous, and infers that religion requires true politeness. The next word defeats everybody. Robertson takes it from a noun for a braggart and calls this the earliest known instance of the verb. Clarke reports that the learned cannot agree whether it is Greek, Latin or Arabic, cites a derivation from the Arabic yielding "is not inconstant," and offers that love does not set itself forward; Calvin says most explain it as acting precipitately and rashly, which is how Wesley takes it, that love never passes a severe sentence on a sudden view of things. Robertson has the next verb from the word for a bellows, love not puffing itself out. On the unseemly, Gill excludes both filthy speech and ludicrous gesture, then gives the opposite reading, that such a person thinks nothing beneath him if it serves, whether making coats for the poor or washing the feet of the saints. Clarke turns on those who claim to be blunt honest men and hold themselves above civility. Ellicott takes thinking no evil as refusing to dwell on the injury done, and Robertson as declining to enter it in a ledger for settlement.
6:
Ellicott makes the attitude of the mind toward sin a great test of whether religious feeling is genuine, and the others treat the clause as a searching one rather than an easy one. Barnes denies that anybody is exempt: men of the world take a malignant pleasure in the report that a professor of religion has disgraced himself, and a man is glad when his persecutor or slanderer utters some rash word that involves him in ignominy. He thinks there is scarcely a greater triumph of the gospel than that it can bring a man to be glad his enemy has done well. Clarke supplies two instances and does not soften either. A man who has forborne revenge and left the matter with God consoles himself, when evil falls on the offender, that his quarrel has been avenged; and interested people rejoice in the successes of an unjust war, their joy always in proportion to the slaughter. If such Christians can be saved, he says, demons need not despair. Robertson notes flatly that there are people whose real joy is in the triumph of evil. Wesley has love weeping at the sin or folly even of an enemy, taking no pleasure in hearing or repeating it, and wishing it forgotten for ever.

Gill turns the same clause inward, to the man who mourns the corruption of his own heart and the secret sins none know but God, and finds his instance in the healing of the ear Peter had cut off, where the injury was done in zeal for Christ and Christ was displeased by it. On what the answering word means, Clarke takes the first term as falsehood, so that love rejoices in everything opposed to falsehood and irreligion and therefore helps true religion forward instead of hindering it; Barnes takes it as virtue and piety, standing opposed to iniquity. The verb that opens the next verse divides them further. Barnes sets out the whole dispute: it properly means to cover, from the word for a roof, and Doddridge, Locke and Macknight so render it, while others make it forbear or endure, the classical usage favouring the first and the New Testament usage the second; he concludes the sense is not materially altered either way. Clarke reports the argument that "cover" must be right because otherwise the clause merely repeats the endurance named later in the same verse, doubts the word will bear it, and prefers to contain or keep in, as a vessel holds liquor.

Robertson keeps the roof and lets it mean all three at once, that love covers, protects and forbears, throwing a veil over a multitude of sins. Gill guards the covering with a condition: the offender is first reproved privately and faithfully and brought to acknowledge the fault, and only then is it hidden from others under the mantle of love. Wesley makes the rule absolute except where duty constrains speech. Calvin enters the sharpest qualification of the group, and enters it twice. Bearing does not mean sanctioning vices by flattery or encouraging them by winking at them, and it does not exclude just punishment; believing does not mean that a Christian knowingly lets himself be imposed upon, or divests himself of prudence, or unlearns how to tell black from white. What is required is candour in judging, and the upshot he states plainly: a Christian will reckon it better to be imposed on by his own easy temper than to wrong his brother by an unfriendly suspicion. Robertson says much the same in four words, not gullible but having faith in men, adds that hope here sees the bright side and does not despair and that endurance carries on like a stout-hearted soldier, and observes that the four cardinal virtues of the Stoics and the three Christian graces are all present in the passage as marks of love.
8:
Chrysostom counts this the third argument for love and reads its purpose as double: to persuade those reckoned inferior that the chief of all signs lies within their reach, so that they are no worse off than the holders of gifts but better, and at the same time to bring down those whom the greater gifts had lifted up, by showing they have nothing without it. Envy and pride are removed together, and a wall thrown round the congregation. Ellicott puts the same contrast in terms of what lasts: the Corinthians were preferring things that are for a time to graces that are for ever, and one faction had exalted above everything the most ephemeral gift of all. Barnes traces the verb from its use of stars falling, flowers fading and chains dropping from the hands, and takes it here as ceasing to be in existence. Henry has love lasting as eternity, heaven being the very seat and element of it, and Clarke that it cannot fall off because it bears and believes and hopes and endures, and that properly speaking it includes the other graces, which take their perfection from it. Robertson says love survives everything, and remarks how little of human work lasts.

Robertson notices that the three verbs are not alike: prophecy and knowledge are to be made inoperative, but the middle voice used of tongues has them ceasing of themselves. Henry identifies what goes: prophecy, whether the foretelling of things to come or the interpreting of scripture by immediate inspiration, and tongues, the power of speaking languages never learnt. There will be one language in heaven, he says, for there is no confusion of tongues in the region of perfect tranquillity, and Wesley says the same, that one speech will prevail among the inhabitants and the low imperfect languages of earth be forgotten. On knowledge Henry is careful. He will not have it that the blessed are ignorant, since a happiness consisting with utter ignorance would be a poor one; the apostle means the knowledge supernaturally communicated, though if the common sort is meant then the way of knowing vanishes while what was learnt is not lost. Wesley and Barnes reach independently for the same image, starlight lost in the light of noon. Ellicott finds a better one: gifts are the implements of the divine husbandry and graces are the seed, so that at harvest the tools are laid aside while the seed is transformed by dying and keeps that form for ever.

Calvin says the next clause is misread by most, who take it to mean that our knowledge is not yet perfect and we are daily improving. His own reading inverts that: it is because we are not yet perfect that we have knowledge and prophecy at all, these being helps to an infirmity, so that when the infirmity ends the helps must end with it, since it would be absurd for them to remain and serve no use. Gill guards the clause from three misuses, denying that it makes the Scriptures incomplete and in want of traditions or fresh revelations, that it confines knowledge to some of the saints, or that only a portion of truth is known at all. Clarke turns it into a comparison, that the man who knows most knows little beside what angels know, and quotes the epigram on Newton, whom superior beings watching him explain all nature's law showed as we show an ape; he adds that the poet took the thought from Plato without acknowledging the debt. Robertson glosses the perfect as the full-grown, and Ellicott holds that the emphatic "then" fixes the time at the close of this dispensation, the imperfect not ceasing until the perfect is brought in. Calvin dates it from death but says it is not fully manifested before the judgment.
11:
Robertson keeps the tenses in view: the three verbs of childhood are imperfects, what the speaker used to do, while becoming a man is a perfect and so a state still standing, and the putting away is another perfect, made inoperative for good. Ellicott presses the same correction of the English, that the sense is not a moment of transition in the past but the present condition of a grown man, and reports the suggestion that the three childish verbs answer one by one to the three gifts, speaking to tongues, understanding to prophecy, reasoning to knowledge; he will not insist on so exact a correspondence, thinking only that the number was naturally made to match. Barnes fixes the age lower than boyhood, at the point where a child is just beginning to articulate, and borrows Doddridge's confession that he was thrown into transports of joy or grief on the slightest occasion, which manly reason afterwards taught him to despise. Clarke says such a creature has few ideas and little beyond instinct, and that less perfect than the brute's. Gill applies the lisping directly to the gift the Corinthians prized, tongues at their highest being child's speech beside what the perfected will say. Calvin observes only that education suits childhood and does not comport with maturity.

Then comes the one place in the chapter where a commentator stands alone against the rest. Barnes argues that the figure is of looking through an imperfect medium rather than at a reflection, since reflection does not suit the obscurity Paul means; he supposes the thin plates of transparent stone the ancients set in windows, the mica Pliny describes, and adds a long account of how glass was found by accident when a ship's crew rested their kettles on lumps of alkali in the sand. Everyone else refuses it. Clarke insists the noun means a mirror and not a glass to look through, that such an image would not have suited the design at all, and produces Anacreon telling his mirror how few of his hairs remain. Ellicott says the same word is used elsewhere of a mirror and that a pane of horn or transparent stone, though such things existed, would have required quite a different word. Robertson notes that ancient mirrors were of polished metal and that those made at Corinth were famous, and Wesley that the glass reflects only imperfect forms, dim and faint, so that our thoughts about them are puzzling and everything is a kind of riddle.

On the second half of the phrase they agree again. Robertson renders it literally as in an enigma and quotes the remark that seeing a friend's face in a cheap mirror is a very different thing from looking at the friend; Calvin says the word properly means a riddle and is so used by the classical writers, and both he and Ellicott take Paul to have had in view the promise of speaking mouth to mouth and not in dark speeches. Calvin then identifies what the mirror is, and the answer is not obvious: the ministry of the word, the means God who is otherwise invisible has appointed for discovering himself, and perhaps the whole frame of the world besides, since angels who see him another way need neither preaching nor sacraments. Gill narrows it to the gospel, holding that God may be seen in the works of creation as the God of nature but not there as the God of grace. Robertson observes that the preposition in "face to face" is used three times over and that the final verb is the compounded one, to know fully. Wesley draws out what that must mean, a knowledge in some measure like God's own, who sees at one glance through the soul and all things.
13:
Ellicott begins by refusing to read the opening word as a mark of time. It is logical rather than temporal, not this present life set against the life to come but the conclusion drawn from everything argued so far. Calvin reads it the same way and gives it a figure from bookkeeping: when every deduction has been made, this is the sum that remains. He notes too that faith is taken more widely here than in the earlier verses, the whole ministry of the church existing to instruct us in these three. Robertson points out that the verb of abiding is singular, agreeing with the first noun in the list, and that the adjective at the end is comparative in form though it does superlative duty, the true superlative having grown rare by then. Barnes takes the verb strictly, of remaining as against being removed or passing away, and holds that the three must therefore outlast everything named in the preceding verses, knowledge included. Gill specifies which faith is meant, not the faith of miracles, which does not abide, nor bare assent to truth, which men may hold for a while, but the faith peculiar to God's elect, and hope as a grace implanted in regeneration.

Whether all three survive into the next state is the chapter's last quarrel. Calvin says plainly that faith does not remain after death, since the apostle elsewhere sets it against sight and makes it last only while we are absent from the Lord; hope he defines as perseverance in faith, so that both belong to a condition of imperfection while love remains in perfection. Wesley states the same conclusion in a sentence, that the three are the sum of perfection on earth and love alone the sum of perfection in heaven. Barnes argues the contrary at length, that the strain of the argument requires faith and hope to subsist in the world where prophecy has ceased, and he lists the commentators ranged against him. Clarke is among the names he lists, and yet Clarke had already rejected that very position, asking whether the apostle says faith is lost in sight and hope in fruition, or whether any inspired man says so, and answering that faith and hope will enter eternal glory as necessarily as love. Ellicott holds the same, that the contrast intended is between ephemeral gifts and enduring graces, and complains that popular hymnody has taught almost the opposite of what was written.

The reasons given for the primacy differ as much as the readings do. Clarke will not rest it on duration at all, since he thinks all three endure; he rests it on likeness, love being properly the image of God in the soul, so that by faith we receive from our Maker and by hope we expect a future good, but by love we resemble him. He adds that faith is the foundation and hope rears the building while love completes and crowns it, that faith and hope respect ourselves alone where love takes in God and man, and that love is called the fulfilling of the law, which is never said of the other two. Barnes also declines the argument from duration, denying that the apostle grounds the primacy on lasting longer, and puts it instead on love mattering more to the welfare of others. Calvin makes the point structurally: every man derives the advantage of his own faith and hope, but love extends its benefits beyond him, and faith itself is elsewhere called an effect of love, the effect being inferior to its cause. Robertson closes by noting that the greatness has been referred to God himself, love being one of his attributes.
